stages.title: Orient and logistics
stages.why: You cannot study well for an exam you are not eligible for, have not booked, or are preparing for with the wrong blueprint.
do: Read the Exam facts page and 'Why you saw 27%'. Discard any trainer built on 27/18/20/20/15.
Confirm your employer is in the Claude Partner Network and that you can register with a company-domain email.
Check your partner tier for a discount, and note that the reschedule deadline is 48 hours before your appointment.
Choose OnVUE or a test centre. If OnVUE, run the Pearson system test now on the machine you will use.
Set an exam date (or choose 'no date yet'), your minutes per day, and a schedule: 2-week, 3-week or 6-week.
stages.exit: The exam date (or 'no date yet') and the schedule are saved, and every item on the logistics checklist is ticked.

stages.title: Self-assess and baseline
stages.why: A measured baseline tells you where the points are. Self-ratings alone miss the objectives you are overconfident about.
do: Rate all 38 objectives R/Y/G. Red: you cannot state the decision rule. Yellow: you know it but are unsure under trade-offs. Green: you can decide a scenario and name the trap (about 15 min).
Work the 3 official Section 8 samples as worked examples: find the constraint, classify it, name each distractor's trap (about 10 min).
Take the 21-item baseline (3 per domain, 4 multi-response) and mark your confidence on each answer (about 40 min).
Review the calibration flags (Overconfident / Underrated / Unmeasured) and accept or edit the suggested re-ratings.
stages.exit: The baseline is submitted, the priority queue is generated, and the re-ratings are confirmed.

stages.title: Foundations gap-fill (conditional)
stages.why: Professional items assume fluency with the API, MCP and Claude Code basics. Without that fluency, judgement items feel like vocabulary tests.
do: Open this stage only if your baseline is below 55% in D2, D3 or D7, or 5 or more objectives are Red.

Take only the prerequisite courses that cover your Red areas: Building with the Claude API, Introduction to MCP and Claude Code in Action first; Claude 101, AI Fluency and AI Capabilities & Limitations only if needed.
Run the Foundations bridge drills. They are for mastery only and never count toward readiness.
Do not study CCAR-F material at CCAR-F weight. Claude Code internals are 7% here.
stages.exit: You score 70% or better on the bridge drills, or the stage is skipped because its trigger was not met.

stages.title: Priority study loop
stages.minutes: 600–1,350 (38 sections at about 10 min each plus interleaved drills is about 600; the 733-minute official prep path adds up to 733 more, less if you take only the courses for your weak domains)
stages.why: This is where most of your score is built. Order the work by weight × gap so the hours go where the points are.
do: Study objective sections in priority order (default D3 > D1 > D4 > D5 = D6 > D2 > D7, re-sorted by your gaps and overconfidence flags).
For each section: pretest, rule, core idea, cue rows, worked example, traps and contrast, self-explain, check, then 'Prove it' and a re-rating.
Pair each domain block with its official course: Course 2 with D3/D4, Course 1 with D1/D2, Course 3 with D5, Course 4 with D6, Course 5 with D7.
After every 3 sections, run a 10-item interleaved mix.
Do due spaced reviews first each day, capped at 40% of the day's minutes.
stages.exit: Every objective is Practised: 4 or more graded items with accuracy of 0.6 or better.

stages.title: Reading and build project (parallel)
stages.why: The official guide tells you to build and run one end-to-end solution. Primary sources give you the vocabulary that the exam's rationales use.
do: Read the primary sources on the Reading list alongside the matching domain block.
Build a small Meridian-style system: RAG over policy text plus a system-of-record lookup for live status.
Add an eval harness with pre-agreed thresholds, a per-slice breakdown and one A/B test whose metric, sample size and stopping rule are fixed in advance.
Add tracing, input and output guardrails, HITL on irreversible actions, and a compliance map linking each obligation to its control, owner and evidence.
Write one ADR and a one-page stakeholder brief with an SLA stated as p95 at peak.
stages.exit: The 8 build artefacts are ticked, or the stage is marked skipped with a reason.

stages.title: Trap mastery
stages.why: Most misses come from a small number of recurring distractor families. Once you can name the trap, you stop falling for it.
do: Open this stage when any trap has 5 or more exposures and a fall rate of 35% or more.
Read the atlas cards and trigger words for your top traps.
Run trap drills, including the name-the-trap question and the counter-trap items where the tempting answer is actually right.
Do the multi-response clinic twice: count first, judge options independently, drop the filler, check the pair's balance.
stages.exit: Every trap with 5 or more exposures has a fall rate under 30%, and multi-response accuracy is 60% or better.

stages.title: Form A and remediation
stages.why: Your first full timed sitting measures readiness on fresh items and shows your pacing under realistic conditions.
do: Sit Form A in strict mode at about 55% of your timeline, once at least 70% of objectives are Practised and no later than T-7, so Form B fits at least 3 days later and Form C by T-3.
Pace at 1:45 per item, using the checkpoints (17/30:00, 34/60:00, 51/90:00, 63/110:00) and the 3-minute flag rule.
Read the score report: expected misses per domain and the traps that cost you points.
Remediate the top 5 weak objectives: reread the cue rows and trap cards, then answer 5 items each.
stages.exit: Form A is submitted, reviewed and remediated.

stages.title: Form B and second remediation
stages.why: A second fresh form shows whether the remediation worked, rather than whether you remembered the items.
do: Sit Form B at least 3 days after Form A.
Run a second remediation pass on your weakest objectives and on any D5 or D6 score below 70%.
If the readiness interval is still wide, add a half mock (32 items) or an adaptive mock.
stages.exit: Readiness shows On track: every domain gate is met and multi-response accuracy is 60% or better.

stages.title: Dress rehearsal
stages.why: Sitting a full exam under real conditions takes the logistics and pacing surprises out of exam day.
do: Unseal Form C and sit it between T-7 and T-3 under exam conditions: one monitor, no phone, no notes, a single sitting.
Rehearse the full timeline, including 15 minutes of pre-exam setup.
Write a final targeted remediation list of no more than 5 objectives.
stages.exit: Readiness shows Ready, or a final remediation list is written.

stages.title: Taper and exam day
stages.minutes: 30–45 per day for the last 3 days
stages.why: Consolidating what you know beats learning new material in the last days, and a rested reader catches constraint words.
do: Learn no new material, and take no sealed form after T-2.
Each day: the night-before cheat-sheet mode, cue flashcards, and clearing the spaced-review queue.
Do one 10-item pacing drill at 1:45 per item.
Recheck the OnVUE system test, make sure your ID name matches your registration, and set up the room.
Exam day: count first on multi-response, flag anything past 3 minutes, keep the last 10 minutes for flags and counts, and answer everything.
stages.exit: The exam is taken, and the score report's domain percentages are logged.

schedules.name: 2-week sprint
schedules.who: Engineers who already ship production LLM systems and whose baseline is mostly Yellow or Green
plan: Day 1: Stages 0–1 (logistics, 38 ratings, 3 official samples, 21-item baseline).
Day 2: D3 Integration, all 8 sections, plus a 10-item mix. Start official Course 2.
Day 3: D1 Solution Design, 6 sections, plus a mix. Start Course 1.
Day 4: D4 Evaluation, 6 sections, plus a mix. Finish Course 2 at 1.5x speed where you are Green.
Day 5: D5 Governance (5) and D6 6.1–6.2. Start Course 3.
Day 6: D6 6.3–6.5, D2 (5) and D7 (3). Skim sections where your rating and baseline agree Green. Skim Courses 4–5.
Day 7: Trap mastery for your top traps, plus the multi-response clinic twice.
Day 8: Form A, timed and strict, then read the score report.
Days 9–10: Remediate the top 5 weak objectives and drill the traps that cost you points.
Day 11: Form B, then a short remediation pass.
Day 12 (T-3): Form C dress rehearsal, or an adaptive mock if Form C was already used.
Days 13–14: Taper only (cheat sheet, flashcards, due reviews, OnVUE check). Day 15: exam.

schedules.name: 3-week standard (default)
schedules.who: Most candidates: architects with some production LLM exposure
plan: Days 1–2: Stages 0–1. Book the exam and note the 48-hour reschedule deadline.
Days 3–5: D3 Integration sections, paired with official Course 2 (Enterprise Integration & Production).
Days 6–7: D1 Solution Design sections, paired with Course 1 (Claude Platform & Solution Design).
Days 8–9: D4 Evaluation sections. Finish Course 2. Build an eval harness with thresholds.
Day 10: D5 Governance sections, paired with Course 3 (Responsible AI, Safety & Risk).
Day 11: D6 Stakeholder sections, paired with Course 4 (Stakeholder Engagement, Lifecycle & GTM).
Day 12: Form A, timed, and review (about 55% of the timeline; D3, D1, D4, D5 and D6, about 30 of 38 objectives, are Practised by now).
Day 13: D2 and D7 sections, paired with Course 5 (Team Enablement), and trap mastery for the traps Form A exposed.
Days 14–15: Remediation (top 5 weak objectives) and the multi-response clinic.
Day 16: Form B. Day 17: second remediation pass, focused on D5 and D6.
Day 18 (T-3): Form C dress rehearsal.
Days 19–20: Taper (no new material). Day 21: exam.

schedules.name: 6-week foundation
schedules.who: Candidates newer to production LLM systems, or with 5 or more Red objectives
plan: Week 1: Stages 0–1. Start Stage 2 with the prerequisite courses for your Red areas (API, MCP, Claude Code in Action) and the bridge drills.
Week 2: D3 and D1 sections with Courses 1–2 (the two heaviest domains, 36% together). Start the build project: RAG plus a system-of-record lookup.
Week 3: D4, D5 and D6 sections with Courses 3–4. Add an eval harness, guardrails, HITL and a compliance map to the build. 14-item check-in (2 per domain).
Week 4: D2 and D7 sections with Course 5, then trap mastery and the multi-response clinic. Form A at the end of the week (about day 24, 57% of the timeline), then its remediation list.

Week 5: Remediation from Form A (write the ADR and stakeholder brief as D6 practice). Form B mid-week (at least 3 days after A), then a second remediation pass. Adaptive or half mocks if the readiness interval is still wide.
Week 6: Form C at T-5 as the dress rehearsal. Final targeted remediation, then taper for the last 3 days: cheat sheet night-before mode, flashcards, one pacing drill. Exam at the end of the week.

prep.title: Responsible AI, Safety & Risk for Architects

reading.title: Claude Certified Architect – Professional Exam Guide v1.0 (PDF)
reading.why: The source of truth for the blueprint: the 7 domains, 38 objectives, format, policies and the 3 official samples. Read it first and again during the taper.

reading.title: Building effective agents
reading.why: The augmented LLM, workflow patterns (chaining, routing, parallelisation, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer) and when an agent is actually justified.

reading.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
reading.why: When multi-agent designs pay off (independent, parallel breadth), what they cost, how to hand context over, and how to evaluate agents.

reading.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents
reading.why: Context as a finite resource: just-in-time retrieval, compaction, structured notes and sub-agent isolation.

reading.title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents
reading.why: Tool design, namespacing, token-efficient responses, and evaluating tools. Explains why a mega-tool and endpoint-per-tool designs both fail.

reading.title: Introducing Contextual Retrieval
reading.why: Chunk context, hybrid lexical plus embedding search, and re-ranking: how to fix precision instead of raising top-k.

reading.title: Code execution with MCP: Building more efficient agents
reading.why: Progressive discovery of tools and keeping intermediate data out of context when there are many MCP servers.

reading.title: Equipping agents for the real world with Agent Skills
reading.why: Skills as on-demand know-how with progressive disclosure, and how they differ from MCP connections.

reading.title: Prompt caching (docs)
reading.why: Prefix order, breakpoint placement, and why content that changes per request invalidates the cache. Sample 2 rests on this.

reading.title: Tool use with Claude (docs)
reading.why: Client and server tools, strict schemas, and the tool-call loop you design authorization around.

reading.title: Tool search tool (docs)
reading.why: Loading tools on demand for large catalogues, the platform answer to tool bloat.

reading.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations (docs)
reading.why: Specific, measurable success criteria, eval design and grader choice (code, human, model), which are the core of D4.

reading.title: Reduce hallucinations (docs)
reading.why: Grounding, quote-first answers, citations and permission to say 'I don't know'.

reading.title: Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections (docs)
reading.why: Layered input screening, harmlessness checks and the principle that guardrails sit outside the model's discretion.

reading.title: Batch processing (docs)
reading.why: Asynchronous, lower-cost processing for non-interactive work, and why it is wrong for anything a user waits on.

reading.title: Citations (docs)
reading.why: Returns the passages that support each claim. Useful for grounded RAG answers and auditability.

reading.title: Context windows (docs)
reading.why: Context budgeting, compaction and context editing. Read principles only; sizes are version-sensitive.

reading.title: Agent Skills overview (docs)
reading.why: Three-level progressive disclosure and the difference between a Skill and MCP.

reading.title: Model Context Protocol specification (latest)
reading.why: Protocol roles, primitives and transports. Read to understand when MCP is the right integration mechanism.

reading.title: MCP specification: Authorization
reading.why: Token audience validation, no token passthrough, and why the model must never decide authorization.

reading.title: Claude Code: Settings files and precedence
reading.why: User, project and managed scopes, and which scope wins. Covers the difference between how far a setting reaches and whether it can be overridden (D7).

reading.title: Claude Code: How Claude remembers your project (memory)
reading.why: CLAUDE.md scopes and what memory can and cannot guarantee.

reading.title: Claude Code: Hooks reference
reading.why: Deterministic enforcement points, the answer when a rule must hold every time.

reading.title: Claude Code: Configure permissions
reading.why: Allow and deny rules and org-wide non-overridable policy, which is least privilege for developer tooling.
